title: What a Home Sale Contingency Means for Buyers and Sellers
content_html:
What Is a Home Sale Contingency?

A home sale contingency is a clause in a purchase agreement that makes a buyer's obligation to complete the purchase of a new home dependent on the buyer first selling (or being under a non-contingent contract to sell) their current home. In plain terms, it tells the seller: "I will buy your house, but only once my own house sells." If the buyer's existing home doesn't sell within the agreed timeframe, the contingency gives the buyer a way to cancel the new purchase and recover their deposit.

This type of contingency is less common in fast-moving, competitive markets, but it still shows up regularly — especially with move-up buyers who have significant equity tied up in their current property and can't qualify for or comfortably afford two mortgage payments at once.

Why Buyers Use a Home Sale Contingency

For many buyers, the equity in their current home is the source of the down payment on the next one. Without a completed sale, they may not have the cash — or the qualifying income ratios — to close on a new purchase. A home sale contingency lets a buyer make an offer on a home they want without having to sell their current property first and risk being temporarily without a place to live, or without having to carry two mortgages simultaneously if the sale is delayed.

It's a way of sequencing two transactions that are, in practice, linked: the money from selling home A is what funds the purchase of home B.

Why Sellers Are Often Cautious About Accepting One

From a seller's perspective, a home sale contingency introduces uncertainty. The seller is effectively agreeing to take their home off the market (or continue showing it with a contingent status) while waiting on a sale they don't control, in a market they aren't party to. If the buyer's home doesn't sell in time, the deal can fall apart, and the seller may have lost weeks or months of marketing time in the process.

Because of this risk, sellers who do accept a home sale contingency often negotiate protections, the most common being a "kick-out" or "release" clause.

The Kick-Out Clause

A kick-out clause allows the seller to keep marketing the home even after accepting a contingent offer. If another buyer comes along with a non-contingent (or otherwise stronger) offer, the seller can notify the original contingent buyer, who then typically has a set number of days — agreed to in the contract — to either remove their home sale contingency and proceed with the purchase, or step aside and let the new buyer take the contract.

This structure gives the seller a way to keep their listing exposed to the market without fully closing the door on the contingent buyer. It's a middle ground: the seller isn't stuck waiting indefinitely, and the original buyer gets a real, if time-limited, chance to firm up their offer if a competing buyer appears.

How a Home Sale Contingency Differs From Other Contingencies

Buyers in California purchase agreements commonly encounter several types of contingencies — inspection, appraisal, and loan contingencies among them. A home sale contingency is distinct because it depends on an entirely separate transaction (the sale of the buyer's current home) rather than on something discovered or verified within the subject property itself, like a defect found during inspection or a loan that doesn't appraise. For a broader look at how contingencies generally function in a California purchase contract, see our guide to contingencies in a California purchase agreement.

Structuring the Timeline

Because two transactions are involved, timing matters a great deal. A buyer's agreement typically specifies a deadline by which the buyer's current home must be in escrow, or fully closed, for the contingency to be satisfied. Sellers negotiating these terms often want the window kept as short as reasonably possible, while buyers want enough runway to market and close their existing home without feeling rushed into underpricing it.

It's also worth remembering that the buyer's own home sale is a transaction with its own contingencies and escrow process. Buyers relying on a home sale contingency should have a realistic sense of what their own closing timeline looks like — our guide to what happens during escrow walks through that process in more detail.

When a Home Sale Contingency Makes Sense

  • Buyers with most of their net worth in home equity: If a down payment depends on sale proceeds, a contingency protects against being contractually obligated to close before that cash is available.
  • Buyers who can't carry two housing payments: A contingency avoids the risk of being on the hook for a new mortgage before the old home sells.
  • Slower-moving markets: Sellers are generally more willing to accept a contingent offer when homes aren't routinely selling with multiple competing bids.

When It's a Harder Sell

  • Competitive, low-inventory markets: Sellers fielding multiple offers have little incentive to accept the uncertainty of a contingent buyer when non-contingent offers are available.
  • Sellers with their own tight timeline: A seller who needs to close by a specific date for their own next purchase may simply decline contingent offers outright.

Buyers in a competitive market who still need to sell first sometimes explore alternatives — a bridge loan, a home equity line against the current property, or simply listing and selling before shopping for the next home — to make their offer non-contingent and more attractive to sellers. For buyers trying to understand how to position an offer competitively in general, our guide to making a competitive offer in Temecula Valley covers additional strategies.

What Sellers Should Weigh Before Accepting

A seller considering a contingent offer should look closely at how far along the buyer's current home sale actually is. An offer contingent on a home that hasn't even been listed yet carries far more uncertainty than one contingent on a home already in escrow with its own contingencies removed. Sellers should also consider the strength of the local resale market for the buyer's property — a buyer's home in a desirable, fast-selling neighborhood is a very different risk proposition than one that may sit on the market for an extended period.

Negotiating a kick-out clause, a reasonable but firm deadline, and clear documentation of the buyer's own home sale progress are the main tools sellers use to manage this risk while still keeping a willing, qualified buyer in play.

Working Through the Details

Every home sale contingency is negotiated individually — the length of the window, whether a kick-out clause applies, what counts as "in escrow" for the buyer's current home, and how deposits are handled if the contingency isn't met are all terms that should be spelled out clearly in writing rather than assumed. Buyers and sellers on either side of this kind of offer benefit from working through the specific language with their agent before signing.
